screens.title: Cost-Performance Trade-offs & Optimization Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore how every architectural choice in AWS carries a cost and a performance impact. You will learn to analyze trade-offs, apply right-sizing, and use purchasing options intentionally so budgets and performance targets align. We’ll emphasize actionable practices: using AWS Compute Optimizer to surface opportunities, selecting appropriate S3 and EBS options for storage, and designing for minimized data transfer. A practical example you’ll see throughout the lesson is choosing instance sizes and purchase types: a larger instance buys headroom but increases cost, whereas a Savings Plan or Spot instance lets you lower spend while keeping capacity available. I’ll also call out common surprises such as cross-AZ transfer fees and idle resources that quietly inflate bills. By the end you should be able to explain why a chosen performance improvement is worth its cost and propose a low-risk plan to implement it. Think about a recent system you manage—what single change could reduce cost without breaking performance?

screens.title: Cost-Performance Trade-offs: definition and framing
screens.narratorSegment: Cost-performance trade-offs mean you must weigh the benefit of improved speed, latency, or reliability against the added expense those improvements bring. Define the desired performance metric first: is it lower latency, higher throughput, or predictable tail latency? Then measure current behavior and map the cost to each improvement. A concrete example: increasing an EC2 instance size often reduces latency but doubles hourly compute cost. An alternative might be horizontal scaling with smaller instances to keep cost per request lower. A common misconception is to assume more expensive equals better; in reality extra capacity is sometimes unused and thus wasted. Another misconception is treating serverless as automatically cheaper; Lambda eliminates instance management but still incurs charges for memory, duration, and attached services and can generate data transfer costs. The practical rule is to make decisions based on measured workload and SLA requirements, not on general rules. Start with small experiments, measure the delta in both performance and cost, and document trade-offs before committing to long-term purchases. What metric would you choose to judge success for a performance change? Cost-Performance Trade-offs: definition and framing means a cost-performance trade-off is an intentional balance: achieve required performance at the lowest practical cost by measuring and choosing the best combination of resources.. In practical terms, why every design decision affects both performance and cost. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: A cost-performance trade-off is an intentional balance: achieve required performance at the lowest practical cost by measuring and choosing the best combination of resources.

content.html:
Core Concept Definition
What this trade-off means
Frame performance goals, measure costs, and choose the right corrective action.
Illustrative example
You have an API that occasionally spikes. Two options: upsizing a single instance, or adding more small instances behind a load balancer.
Vertical scale
Higher single-instance performance, higher per-hour cost, lower operational complexity.
Horizontal scale
Better resilience and cost-per-request optimization, requires load distribution and state design.
Explanation & common misconceptions
  • Assume changes by measurement: collect CPU, memory, and latency before deciding.
  • Serverless is not free: costs come from duration, memory, API Gateway, and data transfer.
  • Don’t buy long-term for short transient peaks; use burstable or autoscaling options.
Key Takeaway

Make measurable decisions: choose the change that meets SLAs for the least added cost and verify with experiments.

screens.title: Right-Sizing: an operational process
screens.narratorSegment: Right-sizing is an ongoing operational process to align resource capacity with workload demand. Start by collecting utilization metrics: C P U, memory, network input and output, and disk input and output. Next, analyze historical patterns and identify underutilized and overutilized resources. Use tools such as AWS Compute Optimizer to get recommended instance types and EBS adjustments. Then, run low-risk experiments: apply changes in a test environment or implement instance type changes during a maintenance window while monitoring performance. A concrete example: an m5. large instance with sustained 10 percent average C P U usage is a candidate to downsize to m5. large? smaller family or a burstable type depending on workload. A common misconception is to right-size only once; instead, incorporate right-sizing into regular operations because workload patterns change. Also avoid chasing short-lived anomalies; use aggregated windows to avoid oscillation. Finally, automate reporting: schedule reports and tag instances for owners to review. This process ensures cost savings while avoiding performance regressions and supports a culture of continuous improvement. keyIdea.title: Right-sizing steps
keyIdea.text: Measure, analyze, act experimentally, monitor results, and repeat. Make it part of routine operations.

content.html:
Process Flow
Right-Sizing Workflow
Step-by-step
  1. Collect utilization metrics for CPU, memory, network and disk.
  2. Group by workload patterns and baseline usage.
  3. Use Compute Optimizer recommendations and validate reason codes.
  4. Test downsizing in staging, monitor SLA metrics, and roll forward when safe.
  5. Automate periodic reviews and tagging for owners.
Example scenario
You run a fleet of instances for background processing. Average CPU per instance is 8% across 30 days, with short daily peaks. Compute Optimizer flags many as overprovisioned.
Action
Move a subset to a smaller family or schedule more aggressive autoscaling.
Outcome
Lower monthly compute cost while keeping peak processing capacity intact.
Key Takeaway

Right-sizing is iterative and must be automated into operations to capture continuous savings without breaking SLAs.

keyIdea.text: Treat recommendations as informed suggestions: validate with tests, understand reason codes, and document decisions before committing.

content.html:
Tooling
Compute Optimizer
Fetch recommendations, inspect reason codes, then validate before applying changes.
CLI example
Run this command to retrieve EC2 recommendations filtered for under- or overprovisioned findings.
aws compute-optimizer get-ec2-instance-recommendations \
    --filters "names=FindingReasonCodes,values=Underprovisioned,Overprovisioned" \
    --max-results 10
The output includes recommended instance types and estimated savings. Use this as a prioritized list for manual review and testing.
Interpreting findings
  • Check the finding reason codes to understand the driver, for example low CPU or inflated I/O.
  • Validate whether peak patterns justify the current instance before downsizing.
  • Test changes in staging and monitor latency and error rates during a controlled window.
Key Takeaway

Use Compute Optimizer to find candidates, but always validate with workload-specific testing and monitoring.

screens.title: Compute purchasing options compared
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding purchasing options is essential to control compute spend while meeting capacity needs. On-Demand instances give full flexibility and are priced highest per hour. Reserved Instances involve a commitment to a specific instance type, region, and term and provide significant discounts up to 72 percent for predictable workloads. Savings Plans provide similar discounts but are more flexible because the commitment applies across instance families, regions, and even different compute services, making them generally preferable for dynamic workloads. Spot Instances offer up to 90 percent off for workloads that can tolerate interruptions, such as batch jobs, CI pipelines, or scalable stateless web tiers. A concrete example: a steady baseline of traffic covered by Savings Plans, short predictable spikes covered with On-Demand, and noncritical background processing scheduled on Spot. A common mistake is buying Reserved Instances for highly variable workloads, which wastes money if usage drops. Always align purchase strategy to workload predictability and implement monitoring to ensure your commitments are being fully utilized. How would you split baseline and burst capacity for a web application? Compute purchasing options compared means choose flexibility for variable workloads and commitments for predictable baselines; use spot for interruptible tasks.. In practical terms, on-demand, reserved instances, savings plans, and spot — strengths and trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Combining purchase models: a practical approach
screens.narratorSegment: A practical purchasing strategy layers different models to optimize cost and reliability. Start with a baseline capacity covered by Savings Plans or Reserved Instances when usage is predictable. This secures a lower effective hourly cost for steady traffic. For unpredictable spikes, keep a pool of On-Demand capacity or autoscaling policies that incur higher per-hour costs but avoid long-term commitments. For interruptible workloads such as batch processing, analytics, or CI runners, use Spot Instances to dramatically reduce cost. A concrete example: allocate Savings Plans for the steady 70 percent of C P U hours, rely on On-Demand autoscaling for sudden 20 percent traffic spikes, and schedule nightly batch jobs on Spot to handle the remaining 10 percent at low cost. A common misconception is that Spot equals unreliability; in practice, a mixed fleet and graceful handling of interruptions preserves completion and reduces cost. The key is visibility: track how commitments are consumed and rebalance when usage patterns change. Ask yourself: what percentage of your compute hours are stable enough for long-term commitment? screens.title: S3 Storage Classes and cost decisions
screens.narratorSegment: Selecting an S3 storage class is a cost decision tied to access frequency and retrieval SLAs. S3 Standard fits frequently accessed data and provides low latency. S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between frequent and infrequent tiers automatically, which is ideal for unknown or changing access patterns though it carries a small monitoring fee. Standard-Infrequent Access and One Zone-IA are lower-cost options for data that is rarely accessed but still needs prompt retrieval; One Zone-IA reduces redundancy for additional savings at the risk of availability if the single zone is impacted. Glacier and Glacier Deep Archive are archival classes with the lowest storage cost and the highest retrieval latency and cost. A concrete example: logs needed for compliance for seven years should move to Glacier Deep Archive after a short retention period because retrieval time in hours is acceptable and storage cost is minimized. A common pitfall is keeping long-term archives in Standard, which is costly. Always align transition policies to retention and retrieval SLAs and test retrieval paths. S3 Storage Classes and cost decisions means match storage class to access frequency and retrieval tolerance; use lifecycle transitions to automate cost savings.. In practical terms, choose the right s3 class for access patterns and retention needs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

S3 Storage Class Selection
Storage class matrix
S3 Standard
Frequent access, low latency, higher cost.

Automatic moves between tiers for unknown patterns; small monitoring fee.

screens.title: EBS volume types and cost considerations
screens.narratorSegment: EBS storage affects both performance and cost. The gp3 volume type lets you provision IOPS and throughput independently from capacity, often giving better price-performance than gp2 for higher input and output requirements. If your workload needs specific IOPS or throughput without more storage, gp3 avoids paying for extra capacity. A concrete scenario: a database that requires higher IOPS but modest storage size can use gp3 and set provisioned IOPS while keeping storage lower, reducing monthly cost compared to a larger gp2 volume sized for IOPS. However, a misconception is to assume gp3 is always cheaper; for low IOPS needs, gp2 may still be simpler and cost-effective. Evaluate actual input and output patterns and test performance under realistic load. Also consider snapshot and lifecycle costs when resizing volumes. The practical step is to monitor IOPS and throughput and move to gp3 when you need fine-grained control over performance, documenting expected savings before committing. EBS volume types and cost considerations means use gp3 to decouple iops from size when i/o needs dominate; validate with workload testing and cost comparison.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use gp3 to decouple IOPS from size when I/O needs dominate; validate with workload testing and cost comparison.

content.html:
Core Concept
EBS: gp3 vs gp2
When to choose gp3
  • When you need predictable IOPS or throughput independent of storage size.
  • When database I/O drives cost more than raw capacity.
  • When resizing to gp3 can avoid paying for unused capacity while delivering required performance.
Example
A DB needs 5,000 IOPS but only 500 GiB storage. Choosing gp3 with provisioned IOPS is often more cost-effective than enlarging a gp2 volume to meet IOPS by size.
Key Takeaway

Select EBS types based on I/O characteristics, not just storage capacity, and measure before changing volumes.

screens.title: Data transfer costs and mitigation strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Data transfer often creates surprising costs if architects do not deliberately design traffic patterns. Inbound data into AWS is generally free, but data egress to the internet and transfers between AZs or regions can be charged. Examples include cross-AZ traffic from load balancers or NAT Gateways, or cross-region replication for S3. To mitigate costs, keep traffic within the same Availability Zone when possible, use VPC endpoints for services like S3 and DynamoDB to avoid internet egress, and plan replication carefully. A concrete example: an application that replicates S3 objects cross-region for DR will incur transfer charges per GB; consider the business need for immediate cross-region replication or use less frequent lifecycle-based replication for archival objects. A common misconception is assuming intra-region traffic is always free; cross-AZ and cross-region transfers often are not. Monitor Cost Explorer for transfer line items, tag flows, and use VPC endpoints and placement strategies to optimize both cost and latency. What transfer flows in your architecture would you audit first? keyIdea.text: Design to minimize cross-AZ and cross-region traffic, use VPC endpoints, and plan replication schedules to reduce egress charges.

content.html:
Problem Area
Data Transfer Costs
Common sources
  • Cross-AZ traffic for NAT Gateways, ALBs, or inter-AZ replication.
  • Cross-region replication for S3 or database replication.
  • Egress to the internet for large datasets or APIs.
Mitigations include using VPC endpoints to keep traffic inside AWS backbone, co-locating services to reduce AZ crossings, and batching or scheduling replication to avoid continuous transfer costs.
Checklist
  1. Audit transfer line items in Cost Explorer.
  2. Identify cross-AZ and cross-region flows.
  3. Apply VPC endpoints where applicable.
Key Takeaway

Design networks and replication for locality; small design choices can eliminate recurring transfer charges.

screens.title: Idle resources and FinOps practices
screens.narratorSegment: Idle resources are low-hanging fruit for cost reduction. Examples include unattached EBS volumes, idle EC2 instances, unused Elastic IPs, and idle RDS instances. Regularly audit with Cost Explorer, Trusted Advisor, and custom scripts to find and remove these resources. Implement schedules to stop non-production environments outside business hours — this often delivers immediate savings versus buying Reserved Instances for rarely used machines. A practical activity: schedule development instances to stop at 6 PM and start at 8 AM Monday to Friday; this saves compute hours and costs only storage while stopped. A common mistake is failing to tag resources or assign owners, which makes cleanup riskier. Adopt a FinOps mindset: create budgets and alerts, require cost allocation tags, and keep a change log for purchases and commitments. Encourage accountability by assigning cost owners and reviewing monthly reports. What policy would you install first to reduce idle cost in your account? Idle resources and FinOps practices means implement audits, schedules, tagging, and budgets to identify idle resources and enable accountable cost control.. In practical terms, detecting waste and adopting budget-conscious operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Operational Practice
Idle Resources & FinOps
Common idle resources
  • Unattached EBS volumes and AMIs kept without owners.
  • Development instances running 24/7 instead of scheduled times.
  • Idle RDS or read replicas kept for testing but not used.
FinOps checks
Apply budgets and alerts, enforce cost allocation tags, schedule non-production shutdowns, and assign cost owners to resource groups. Run monthly reviews and act on orphaned resources.
Key Takeaway

Governance and automation convert recommendations into sustained savings; make cost accountability part of operations.

screens.title: Activity: Analyze Compute Optimizer recommendations & Cost Explorer
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity guides you through a focused audit. First, ensure you have a few EC2 instances running long enough to generate CloudWatch metrics, typically 24 to 48 hours. Enable Compute Optimizer if not already active and wait for recommendations. Pull EC2 recommendations from the CLI or console and sort by estimated monthly savings. Then open Cost Explorer and group by instance type and service to spot where costs concentrate. A concrete runbook: identify instances flagged Overprovisioned, examine their usage graphs for sustained low C P U or idle memory, and select a safe candidate for downsizing in staging. Schedule a maintenance window and apply the change during low traffic while monitoring latency and error rates. For non-production, implement schedule-based automation to stop instances outside working hours. A misconception is assuming every recommended downsizing is safe; always validate with workload-specific tests. After the activity, record the before-and-after cost and performance metrics and update tags and runbooks. content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Audit & Act: Compute Optimizer + Cost Explorer
Starter CLI snippet
aws compute-optimizer get-ec2-instance-recommendations \ 
  --filters "names=FindingReasonCodes,values=Underprovisioned,Overprovisioned" \ 
  --max-results 10
Use this output to build a prioritized review list and validate each candidate in staging before production change.
Checklist
  1. Enable Compute Optimizer and wait for recommendations.
  2. Use Cost Explorer to group costs by instance type and service.
  3. Validate recommendations with tests and roll out changes during low traffic.
Reflection

Document outcomes and track savings to build organizational confidence for further optimization.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: This summary highlights the core concepts you should carry forward. First, cost-performance trade-offs require measurable decisions: define metrics, measure existing behavior, and choose changes that give the best value. Second, right-sizing is an iterative practice supported by Compute Optimizer and monitoring; recommendations are starting points that require validation. Third, purchasing options vary by flexibility and savings: On-Demand for flexibility, Reserved Instances for predictable workloads, Savings Plans for cross-family flexibility, and Spot for interruptible tasks. Fourth, storage and transfer choices matter: select S3 classes and EBS types based on access and input and output patterns, and design to reduce cross-AZ and cross-region transfer. Finally, idle resources and governance are recurring sources of waste; adopt FinOps practices such as tagging, budgets, and scheduled automation. Keep asking whether a performance improvement justifies its ongoing cost, and document the decision to enable accountable trade-offs.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore how every architectural choice in AWS carries a cost and a performance impact. You will learn to analyze trade-offs, apply right-sizing, and use purchasing options intentionally so budgets and performance targets align. We’ll emphasize actionable practices: using AWS Compute Optimizer to surface opportunities, selecting appropriate S3 and EBS options for storage, and designing for minimized data transfer. A practical example you’ll see throughout the lesson is choosing instance sizes and purchase types: a larger instance buys headroom but increases cost, whereas a Savings Plan or Spot instance lets you lower spend while keeping capacity available. I’ll also call out common surprises such as cross-AZ transfer fees and idle resources that quietly inflate bills. By the end you should be able to explain why a chosen performance improvement is worth its cost and propose a low-risk plan to implement it. Think about a recent system you manage—what single change could reduce cost without breaking performance?

By the end of this chapter you will analyze and act on cost-performance trade-offs. Objective one focuses on diagnosing where performance needs justify higher spend and where savings are possible without harm. A practical example is deciding whether to increase instance size to remove a C P U bottleneck or redesign the workload to run horizontally. Objective two teaches right-sizing for EC2, RDS, and Lambda using utilization metrics and AWS Compute Optimizer. You will learn to read findings and turn them into low-risk changes. Objective three covers purchasing options: when to use On-Demand for flexibility, Reserved Instances or Savings Plans to reduce baseline spend, and Spot Instances for interruptible workloads. You will practice combining these for steady-state, spikes, and batch jobs. Objective four covers storage and transfer: choose S3 classes and EBS types, and design to avoid cross-AZ or cross-region transfer charges. Each objective links to a competency milestone so you can demonstrate applied judgement in real accounts.

These objectives continue with practical tool use and governance. You will learn to use AWS Compute Optimizer to generate right-sizing suggestions for EC2, EBS, Lambda, and Auto Scaling Groups, and to interpret 'finding reason codes' so you only apply safe changes. You will understand when Savings Plans outperform Reserved Instances because they span instance families and regions. You will practice identifying data transfer cost hotspots and learn mitigation patterns such as VPC endpoints and keeping traffic within an Availability Zone when possible. Finally, you will adopt a FinOps habit: set budgets and alerts, tag resources, and schedule non-production environments to stop when idle. A concrete example: scheduling development instances to stop outside business hours cuts compute bills drastically versus buying Reserved Instances for fragile, intermittent workloads. These competencies help you protect budget without sacrificing performance engineering practices.

Cost-performance trade-offs mean you must weigh the benefit of improved speed, latency, or reliability against the added expense those improvements bring. Define the desired performance metric first: is it lower latency, higher throughput, or predictable tail latency? Then measure current behavior and map the cost to each improvement. A concrete example: increasing an EC2 instance size often reduces latency but doubles hourly compute cost. An alternative might be horizontal scaling with smaller instances to keep cost per request lower. A common misconception is to assume more expensive equals better; in reality extra capacity is sometimes unused and thus wasted. Another misconception is treating serverless as automatically cheaper; Lambda eliminates instance management but still incurs charges for memory, duration, and attached services and can generate data transfer costs. The practical rule is to make decisions based on measured workload and SLA requirements, not on general rules. Start with small experiments, measure the delta in both performance and cost, and document trade-offs before committing to long-term purchases. What metric would you choose to judge success for a performance change? Cost-Performance Trade-offs: definition and framing means a cost-performance trade-off is an intentional balance: achieve required performance at the lowest practical cost by measuring and choosing the best combination of resources.. In practical terms, why every design decision affects both performance and cost. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Right-sizing is an ongoing operational process to align resource capacity with workload demand. Start by collecting utilization metrics: C P U, memory, network input and output, and disk input and output. Next, analyze historical patterns and identify underutilized and overutilized resources. Use tools such as AWS Compute Optimizer to get recommended instance types and EBS adjustments. Then, run low-risk experiments: apply changes in a test environment or implement instance type changes during a maintenance window while monitoring performance. A concrete example: an m5. large instance with sustained 10 percent average C P U usage is a candidate to downsize to m5. large? smaller family or a burstable type depending on workload. A common misconception is to right-size only once; instead, incorporate right-sizing into regular operations because workload patterns change. Also avoid chasing short-lived anomalies; use aggregated windows to avoid oscillation. Finally, automate reporting: schedule reports and tag instances for owners to review. This process ensures cost savings while avoiding performance regressions and supports a culture of continuous improvement. AWS Compute Optimizer collects historical utilization and suggests changes that reduce cost or improve performance. It analyzes EC2 instances, EBS volumes, Lambda functions, and Auto Scaling Groups and provides findings like Overprovisioned or Underprovisioned with reason codes. A concrete example: you run the CLI command to retrieve recommendations filtered by reason codes to see immediate actionable items. Use the recommendations as a starting point — validate sampling windows and whether your workload has seasonal behavior. A common mistake is to apply a recommendation blindly; instead, review the estimated monthly savings, validate application performance in test, and ensure compatibility with instance families. Understanding purchasing options is essential to control compute spend while meeting capacity needs. On-Demand instances give full flexibility and are priced highest per hour. Reserved Instances involve a commitment to a specific instance type, region, and term and provide significant discounts up to 72 percent for predictable workloads. Savings Plans provide similar discounts but are more flexible because the commitment applies across instance families, regions, and even different compute services, making them generally preferable for dynamic workloads. Spot Instances offer up to 90 percent off for workloads that can tolerate interruptions, such as batch jobs, CI pipelines, or scalable stateless web tiers. A concrete example: a steady baseline of traffic covered by Savings Plans, short predictable spikes covered with On-Demand, and noncritical background processing scheduled on Spot. Always align purchase strategy to workload predictability and implement monitoring to ensure your commitments are being fully utilized. This summary highlights the core concepts you should carry forward. First, cost-performance trade-offs require measurable decisions: define metrics, measure existing behavior, and choose changes that give the best value. Second, right-sizing is an iterative practice supported by Compute Optimizer and monitoring; recommendations are starting points that require validation. Third, purchasing options vary by flexibility and savings: On-Demand for flexibility, Reserved Instances for predictable workloads, Savings Plans for cross-family flexibility, and Spot for interruptible tasks. Fourth, storage and transfer choices matter: select S3 classes and EBS types based on access and input and output patterns, and design to reduce cross-AZ and cross-region transfer. Finally, idle resources and governance are recurring sources of waste; adopt FinOps practices such as tagging, budgets, and scheduled automation. Keep asking whether a performance improvement justifies its ongoing cost, and document the decision to enable accountable trade-offs.

A common trap is one-off optimization that is not institutionalized; without process and ownership, regressions happen and savings evaporate.
